findings.message: spec.md excludes the never-requested state ("The display begins only after a review is requested; a never-requested state is outside this ticket"). The ticket, non-goals.md, and boundaries.md say nothing about this state, so the exclusion is a plan-authored narrowing of accepted scope rather than a user-owned boundary. It is nonblocking because no accepted Rule requires that state, but it should be recorded as an unresolved product decision or accepted in the ticket rather than listed under settled scope while "Unresolved product decisions: none" is also claimed.

spec.md states the viewer-permission point twice with different epistemic status: under Builder outcomes it asserts flatly that "no new viewer-permission refusal applies to this existing CLI command", while Evidence and decisions labels the same point an assumption. Surfaces and non-goals neither confirm nor deny a permission gate on the existing status command. The assumption label appears correct; the outcome line should carry the same qualifier so an unsupported claim is not read as a known fact.

spec.md confines the stale-approval rule to a receipt for a different review job or different plan bytes, and states a stale approval never changes the current review to Approved. This is consistent with principles.md keeping the existing authenticated receipt as the only approval authority, and it closes the path where a prior receipt could display as current approval.

The Pending/Rejected boundary is stated behaviorally (Rejected requires a concluded review with blocking findings; interruption and missing receipt stay Pending with the actual error) without specifying implementation design or task sequencing, so the plan stays within Product Plan required content and avoids prohibited content.

spec.md declares "a never-requested state is outside this ticket", but neither the ticket, scenarios.md, nor boundaries.md names that exclusion. The ticket goal ("a builder can distinguish Pending, Approved, and Rejected plan reviews") plausibly covers only post-request states, and all six accepted scenarios begin after a review is requested, so the narrowing is reasonable — but accepted scope and exclusions belong to the user. Recommend the user confirm this exclusion in .project/tickets/CAP100/ticket.md rather than letting it originate in the plan.

Epistemic status is inconsistent between two sections of spec.md. Under "Builder outcomes" the refusal line asserts flatly that "no new viewer-permission refusal applies to this existing CLI command", while "Evidence and decisions" labels the same point an assumption ("the existing CLI command adds no new viewer-permission gate"). surfaces.md supports only that the surface is an existing CLI status command, not that no permission gate exists on it. Restate the refusal line as assumption-qualified so an unsupported claim is not read as a known fact.

The stale-approval rule is stated before it is defined: "A stale approval never changes the current review to Approved" precedes "A stale approval is a receipt for a different review job or different plan bytes." The definition is adequate and discriminating — it covers both the different-job and different-bytes cases that scenario 4 depends on — but ordering the definition first would remove an avoidable ambiguity for scenario authors.

Scenario-coverage adequacy is deliberately not assessed here; that verdict belongs to scenario review after Product approval. Noted only because scenarios.md was supplied as context and its six entries appear to track the plan's stated outcomes.

spec.md Accepted behavior: "A running review shows its running state" sits inside the Pending definition without saying whether running is displayed as Pending or as a distinct label. Read in context it is a sub-detail of Pending, but a second reasonable reading introduces a fourth user-visible status. The ticket accepts three statuses and scenarios.md item 1 requires an unfinished current review to display Pending, so the ambiguity should be resolved by stating that running is presented within Pending. It cannot cause a false Approved or a fabricated rejection, so it is non-blocking.

spec.md defines staleness only for approval receipts ("a receipt for a different review job or different plan bytes"). The Rejected definition is keyed to "the current review" and the observable done state requires only actual blocking findings, so a prior job's findings are already excluded by that wording, but the plan never states the symmetric staleness rule for reviewer verdicts. After the repair-and-retry path in scenarios.md item 4, making the verdict-side staleness rule explicit would remove the need to infer it from the word "current".

context surfaces.md names "status --help" as the existing help entrypoint of the affected CLI command. The plan changes the status display and retry path without saying whether the help text describing available statuses changes. Help text is not named in the ticket goal or accepted scenarios, so this is informational and not an in-scope omission.
spec.md states "No quantitative target is promised," which correctly avoids an unsupported performance or latency claim for the status display. Noted as a supported epistemic choice, not a defect.

spec.md omits the accepted Rejected outcome. The ticket goal requires a builder to distinguish Pending, Approved, and Rejected, with rejected reviews showing the actual blocking findings and permitting repair and retry. The plan's Accepted behavior section defines only Pending and Approved, and names no rejection state, no findings display, and no repair/retry path. Trigger: a completed review with blocking findings. Consequence: the plan permits an implementation that shows such a review as Pending (not finished) or Approved, and shipping it would violate the accepted goal while satisfying every stated behavior in the plan.

spec.md defines Pending as "the review has not finished," which conflicts with the accepted boundary that a finished review without a valid approval receipt stays Pending with its actual receipt error and a retry action, and that an interrupted review stays Pending with its actual error. Under the plan's definition, those two finished-or-aborted states are not Pending, and since the plan's Approved definition keys only on an authenticated approval receipt, a finished review lacking one falls into no defined state at all. Two reasonable implementations follow — one surfacing an invented rejection, one surfacing Approved or an undefined state — and at least one violates the accepted boundary that neither condition invents rejection findings and that approval authority remains the authenticated receipt.

The Observable done state ("A builder can distinguish Pending from Approved") can report the accepted user-facing claim as satisfied while it is false. It is satisfiable with zero Rejected support, no actual blocking findings, and no retry path, so it is non-discriminating proof for the accepted goal: the claimed behavior can be broken while the stated done state still passes.

The Product Plan carries no outcome inventory for the accepted Builder persona. Success and approval outcomes are partially covered, but refusal (blocking findings), failure (interrupted review, invalid receipt), trust (receipt authenticity and staleness), and recovery (repair and retry without changing plan bytes) outcomes are neither described nor marked inapplicable with a specific reason.

spec.md does not keep known facts, assumptions, and unresolved product decisions visibly distinct. Statements such as the Pending and Approved definitions are asserted flatly with no cited support and no separation from open product choices, so a reader cannot tell which boundaries are settled.

Scope and exclusions are consistent with .project/non-goals.md and the ticket (no new approval authority, status store, or notification channel), and the plan contains no implementation design or delivery sequencing. No out-of-scope addition was identified. Scenario coverage against .project/tickets/CAP100/scenarios.md is not adjudicated here; that belongs to scenario review after Product approval.

spec.md omits the Rejected outcome entirely. The accepted ticket goal states a builder can distinguish Pending, Approved, and Rejected, and that rejected reviews show the actual blocking findings and permit repair and retry. The Accepted behavior section lists only Pending and Approved, and Scope and exclusions excludes only new approval authority and notifications, so Rejected is neither defined nor excluded. Triggering condition: a completed review with blocking findings. Observable consequence: the plan permits an implementation that renders such a review as Pending or Approved, so the builder never sees the blocking findings or the repair-and-retry path the accepted goal requires.

spec.md defines "Pending means the review has not finished," which excludes the accepted condition in which a review HAS finished but has no valid approval receipt. The ticket requires that condition to stay Pending with its actual receipt error and a retry action, inventing no rejection findings. The contract is silent on that case, permitting two reasonable implementations: one that keeps it Pending with the real error, and one that treats it as Approved (the review finished) or synthesizes rejection findings. The second falsely reports the accepted user-facing claim, and reading "finished" as approval violates the accepted invariant in .project/principles.md that authenticated receipts are the only approval authority.

spec.md contains no outcome inventory for the accepted Builder persona. Only a success outcome (Approved) and an in-progress outcome (Pending) appear. Refusal (completed review with blocking findings), failure (interrupted review), trust (absent or invalid approval receipt), and recovery (retry without changing plan bytes; a stale approval cannot approve a repaired plan) outcomes are neither specified nor marked inapplicable with a specific reason. The omission permits materially different shipped behavior on each of those paths while still satisfying the plan as written.

The Observable done state, "A builder can distinguish Pending from Approved," is non-discriminating proof for the accepted goal. The claimed behavior can be broken — no Rejected state, no actual blocking findings, no actual error text on interruption, no retry action, a stale approval honored after repair — while this done state still holds. A done state that cannot fail when the accepted behavior is violated cannot gate the behavior decision.

spec.md does not keep known facts, assumptions, and unresolved product decisions visibly distinct, which the Product Plan contract requires as content. Every statement is asserted flatly. Specifically, whether a finished-without-receipt review surfaces the underlying receipt error verbatim or a generic message, and what the retry affordance is on the status surface, are unresolved product choices that are either absent or presented as settled, so downstream scenario definition cannot tell which statements are supported.

spec.md names the surface as "the CLI review status display," while .project/surfaces.md names the accepted surface as the existing CLI status command with help entrypoint `status --help`. The looser phrasing does not by itself authorize a different surface, but the accepted entrypoint is left unstated in the owning plan.

Scope and exclusions restates the .project/non-goals.md boundary on new approval authority and notifications but omits the accepted "no new status store" non-goal. Non-blocking: nothing in the plan proposes new storage.

Scenario coverage is not adjudicated here. .project/tickets/CAP100/scenarios.md is untrusted supporting context and scenario review follows Product approval; the scenarios are cited only as evidence of the accepted behavior boundary the plan must define.

spec.md omits the Rejected outcome, which is inside the accepted ticket scope. The ticket goal states "A builder can distinguish Pending, Approved, and Rejected plan reviews in the CLI. Rejected reviews show the actual blocking findings and permit repair and retry." The Product Plan defines only Pending ("the review has not finished") and Approved ("an authenticated approval receipt"), and excludes nothing that would justify the omission (its exclusions name only new approval authority and notifications). A completed review with blocking findings therefore has no defined accepted behavior: an implementation could map it to Pending, or display it without the actual findings, and still satisfy every statement in the plan while the ticket goal is unmet. This is an in-scope omission that permits materially different shipped behavior.

spec.md leaves the failure and recovery outcomes undefined for the accepted Builder persona. The ticket requires that "An interrupted review or a finished review without a valid approval receipt stays Pending with its actual error and a retry action; neither condition invents rejection findings." The plan's two definitions do not cover a finished review lacking a valid receipt: it is not "not finished" (so not Pending by the plan's own wording) and has no authenticated receipt (so not Approved). Two reasonable implementations follow — one shows Pending with the actual receipt error, another shows Rejected with invented or empty findings — and the second violates the ticket's explicit prohibition. The plan also never states the actual-error display or the retry action, so a conforming implementation can strand the builder with no repair path.

The Observable done state ("A builder can distinguish Pending from Approved") is non-discriminating as acceptance proof for the accepted goal. Rejected display with actual findings, the repair-and-retry path, the stale-approval trust boundary (scenarios.md item 4), and the no-invented-findings constraint can all be broken while this stated done state is fully satisfied. A done state that can report success while the accepted user-facing claim — builders can distinguish and act on all three current review states — is false does not establish the behavior is ready for scenario definition.

spec.md does not keep supported facts, assumptions, and unresolved product decisions visibly distinct; every statement is presented as settled fact with no stated support. In particular, the scoping claim "Only the status display changes" is asserted without support, and the treatment of a review whose receipt validation fails is an unresolved product decision that the plan presents as if already decided by omission.

The consequential outcome inventory for the accepted Builder persona is incomplete and no outcome is marked inapplicable with a specific reason. Success (Approved) and an in-progress state (Pending) are covered; refusal, failure, trust, and recovery outcomes are neither defined nor explicitly excluded, despite personas.md stating the builder needs "actual rejection findings, and a repair and retry path."

The named surface is consistent with supporting context: surfaces.md identifies the existing CLI status command as the only affected surface, and boundaries.md confirms no parent, milestone, or architecture record adds further scope. No out-of-scope addition was found — the plan's exclusions align with non-goals.md and principles.md, which keep existing authenticated receipts as the only approval authority. The defects above are all in-scope omissions, not scope expansion.

Contract-value ambiguity in the failure path: 'Contracts, failure behavior, and proof' states the CLI status contract has exactly Pending, Approved, and Rejected, then says a failed status read 'reports unavailable state'. It is not decided whether 'unavailable' is a fourth displayed value or an error channel alongside one of the three. This is non-blocking because the spec's two Pending-bearing failure conditions (interrupted review, finished-without-valid-receipt) are each decided explicitly as Pending with the actual error and retry, so the residual read-failure path cannot divert an accepted scenario, and both readings preserve the load-bearing invariant that no failure reports Approved. Resolving the wording would remove the ambiguity.

Help-text proof is unnamed: surfaces.md records 'status --help' as the existing help entrypoint of the affected surface, and Doc impact commits to updating the CLI status help text, but the proof strategy names no check over that help output. This is non-blocking because status --help is an existing entrypoint rather than a new one, so the new-entry-point wiring-proof obligation is not triggered, and the help text carries no status-authority behavior. Consider whether the help outcome deserves a named proof or an explicit justified skip.

Surface proof for the help entrypoint is implicit. surfaces.md names the existing CLI status command and identifies `status --help` as its existing help entrypoint, and the plan takes on a Doc impact obligation to update the CLI status help text. The proof strategy exercises the six scenarios through the real CLI and coordinator boundary but does not name credible proof or an explicit justified skip for the help entrypoint itself. This is a warning rather than an error because `status --help` is an existing entrypoint, not a new one requiring real wiring proof, and a stale help string cannot cause a false Approved, a false Rejected, or a suppressed blocking finding. Naming either a cheap help-output assertion or a justified skip would close the surfaces obligation.

The mapping between a failed status read and the declared status contract is left undecided. The plan states the CLI status contract has exactly Pending, Approved, and Rejected, then states that a failed status read reports unavailable state rather than inventing approval. It is not decided whether "unavailable" is a fourth user-visible label, a non-status error channel alongside the existing exit codes, or a presentation of Pending with an error. The accepted safety property is preserved under every reading, since none of them yields Approved or synthesized rejection findings, so this does not block. It is also distinct from the spec'd interrupted and receipt-missing cases, which the plan correctly maps to Pending with the actual error and a retry action. Deciding the form of the unavailable report in the plan would avoid leaving the choice to delivery.

The decision record closes with "No load-bearing external library choice is needed," which reads as a skip scoped to third-party dependency evidence rather than a claim that the plan makes no load-bearing choice. That reading is consistent with the plan's own load-bearing choices, which are recorded inline with the rejected alternative and its reason, so the skip does not contradict the plan. Scoping the sentence explicitly to external dependencies would remove the ambiguity. No evidence records are attached to this review because the plan cites no external research, library, or version-dependent source whose license, security, privacy, or reuse limits would need to be recorded.

Proof coverage for the named help entrypoint is implicit. The surfaces context names 'status --help' as the existing help entrypoint of the affected surface, and Doc impact commits to updating the CLI status help text, but the proof strategy exercises only the six status scenarios and states neither a proof nor an explicit justified skip for the help output. This is non-blocking because the Product Plan promises no help-text behavior, so no accepted user-facing claim can be falsely reported as satisfied; Execution Planning can attach the check when it sequences the doc obligation.

Minor tension between the stated status contract and the read-failure behavior. 'Contracts, failure behavior, and proof' says the CLI status contract has exactly Pending, Approved, and Rejected, then says a failed status read 'reports unavailable state'. Two reasonable implementations follow (a distinct unavailable presentation outside the three labels, or a mapping into Pending with the read error). Non-blocking because both satisfy the accepted claims: neither can display Approved without a current authenticated receipt and neither invents rejection findings. Naming which one is intended would remove the ambiguity before delivery sequencing.

Approach decisions contain: "The reviewer output verdict is enough to display Approved, even before an authenticated approval receipt exists." This conflicts with (a) spec.md accepted behavior "Approved means the current review has an authenticated approval receipt" and "only the authenticated receipt for the current job and plan bytes can display Approved", (b) .project/principles.md "Existing authenticated receipts remain the only approval authority", (c) .project/non-goals.md and the ticket's "No new approval authority ... is in scope", and (d) the plan's own Contracts section, which states "Missing or stale receipt means no approval." Triggering condition: a reviewer concludes with a nonblocking verdict while the approval receipt is absent, unauthenticated, or bound to different plan bytes. Observable consequence: the CLI displays Approved with no authenticated receipt, elevating reviewer output into a new approval authority and falsely reporting the accepted user-facing approval claim. The internal contradiction also leaves two reasonable implementations (verdict-driven vs receipt-driven Approved), and the verdict-driven one additionally collides with accepted scenario 6, which requires a finished nonblocking review without a valid receipt to display Pending with its actual receipt error. Missing or incorrect decision: the single authority that may produce Approved. Accepted decision owner: the user, via the ticket and Product Plan, which already decided it is the authenticated receipt. Action that resumes review: remove this decision and state that only a valid authenticated approval receipt bound to the current job identifier and plan digest may display Approved, with every other finished state mapping to Pending plus its actual error.

spec.md states "A running review shows its running state", while the plan states only "A running review displays Pending." Pending is the correct status bucket, but the plan does not decide whether the running sub-state is conveyed to the builder, leaving that presentation detail to be invented during delivery. Non-blocking because accepted scenario 1 requires only Pending.

Doc impact names an update to the CLI status help text, and .project/surfaces.md identifies `status --help` as the existing help entrypoint of the affected surface, but the proof strategy covers only the six status scenarios through the CLI and coordinator boundary. The help-text change has neither named proof nor an explicit justified skip. Non-blocking because it is documentation on an existing entrypoint rather than a new entry point.

Approach decision 'The reviewer output verdict is enough to display Approved, even before an authenticated approval receipt exists' violates the accepted approval authority and contradicts the plan's own contract. Accepted sources: ticket.md ('Approval still requires the existing authenticated approval receipt'), spec.md ('Approved means the current review has an authenticated approval receipt' and 'only the authenticated receipt for the current job and plan bytes can display Approved'), principles.md ('Existing authenticated receipts remain the only approval authority'), and scenario 6 ('A finished nonblocking review without a valid receipt displays Pending'). The same plan's contract section states 'Missing or stale receipt means no approval', and a later approach bullet states that a finished nonblocking review without a valid receipt displays Pending. Triggering condition: a review finishes with a nonblocking verdict and the approval receipt is missing, unauthenticated, or bound to different plan bytes. Observable consequence: the decision bullet and the contract line permit two reasonable implementations, and one displays Approved with no authenticated receipt — a false user-facing approval claim and a new approval authority that non-goals.md excludes. Missing/incorrect decision: the receipt-independent Approved condition. Decision owner: the Implementation Plan author, bounded by the user-owned ticket and spec, which have already decided this behavior and leave the author no latitude to widen it. Required repair: delete the verdict-sufficient Approved decision and state a single Approved condition — a current, authenticated approval receipt bound to the current job identifier and current plan digest — so the approach decisions, the contract section, and scenario 6 agree. Leaving it unresolved means the proof for scenarios 2 and 6 cannot discriminate between a conforming implementation and one that approves on verdict alone.

spec.md states 'A running review shows its running state', but the plan reduces every unfinished review to 'A running review displays Pending' without naming whether the running detail is surfaced alongside the Pending label. The plan does name the error text and retry action for the interrupted and receipt-missing cases, so this is a presentation-detail gap rather than an omitted decision; name the running-state consequence explicitly so scenario 1's proof can assert more than the bare label.

The contract is declared as 'exactly Pending, Approved, and Rejected', yet the plan also describes a failed status read reporting 'unavailable state'. Unavailable is plausibly an error path outside the three-value status rather than a fourth value, but the plan does not say which. Clarify whether unavailable is a status value or a separate read-failure outcome so the CLI contract stays unambiguous; the accepted scenarios do not cover this path, so it is non-blocking.

Approval authority decision contradicts accepted scope and is self-inconsistent. The Approach decision states "The reviewer output verdict is enough to display Approved, even before an authenticated approval receipt exists," while the same plan's contract section states "Missing or stale receipt means no approval" and "Authorization stays with the existing authenticated receipt." spec.md accepts only "Approved means the current review has an authenticated approval receipt"; ticket.md states "Approval still requires the existing authenticated approval receipt" and excludes any "new approval authority"; principles.md states "Existing authenticated receipts remain the only approval authority." Missing/incorrect decision: which single input authorizes the Approved display. Accepted decision owner: the user, via the authoritative ticket and Product Plan — which already decided it is the authenticated receipt. Consequence of leaving it unresolved: the omitted contract permits two reasonable implementations, and the verdict-driven one displays Approved for a review with no authenticated receipt, falsely reporting the accepted user-facing claim and defeating scenario 6 (finished nonblocking review without a valid receipt must display Pending). It also breaks scenario 4's stale-approval protection in the window before a receipt exists. Resumption action: delete the verdict-sufficiency decision from the Approach section and state that only a current authenticated approval receipt bound to the current job identifier and plan digest displays Approved; a blocking verdict drives Rejected and a nonblocking verdict without a valid receipt drives Pending with the actual receipt error.

The contract declares "exactly Pending, Approved, and Rejected," then adds that a failed status read "reports unavailable state rather than inventing approval." That read-failure output is not mapped onto one of the three declared statuses, so the displayed state for an unreadable coordinator record is ambiguous. Non-blocking: the safe direction (never Approved) is stated, and no accepted scenario covers status-read failure. Naming whether read failure renders as Pending-with-error or as a distinct non-status message would close it.

The decision entry rests on one named alternative (persisting a separate CLI status) with a recorded reason for its loss, and declares no load-bearing external library choice. That skip is consistent with the plan's own load-bearing choices, which are all internal to the existing CLI and coordinator, so no target-version, license, or security evidence baseline is required.

The enumerated RED assertions in Slice 1 are predominantly negative (stale receipt, wrong digest, unauthenticated verdict, failed read must all remain non-Approved). They do not separately name the positive case for accepted scenario 2 (a current authenticated receipt displays Approved) or scenario 1 (a running, unfinished current review displays Pending). These remain covered because the completion signal requires all six accepted scenarios to pass through the CLI entry point and checklist row status-4 obligates proving all six through the CLI and coordinator, and the accepted scenarios file enumerates them exactly, so nothing is left to the implementer to invent. Naming both positive assertions explicitly in the fixture step would remove any reliance on resolving that reference.

Slice 1 packs the mapper, CLI wiring, help-text update, and compatibility assertions into one slice. This is consistent with the conceptual-reviewability standard: all edits serve the single outcome of displaying the current review status, and the help text is the documentation face of that same outcome rather than an independently valuable second purpose.

Data and measurement categories are recorded as inapplicable by the accepted Implementation Plan (no store, schema, ownership, retention, migration, or cross-system flow change; no quantitative target promised). The checklist still carries a data and compatibility row (status-5) bound to the real coordinator-record and exit-code compatibility assertions, so the inapplicability does not drop accepted behavior.

Slice 1 explicitly encodes an empty prerequisite list ("Slice prerequisites: none") and asserts relies_on_unmerged_successor: false; with a single slice there is no forward dependency, cycle, or intermediate-merge hazard.

The help-text obligation (status-9) is not left to a post-proof edit: the plan requires the status --help assertion naming Pending, Approved, and Rejected to live in the same integration fixture and to be rerun after the final help-text edit, so documentation cannot drift past the passing proof.

The RED narrative enumerates the adversarial cases (stale/foreign receipt, unauthenticated verdict, crash before binding, failed read, exit codes, byte-identical records) in detail but does not individually name the positive assertions for scenario 1 (unfinished current review displays Pending) and scenario 2 (current authenticated receipt displays Approved). Coverage is still bound by the completion signal ("all six accepted scenarios pass through the CLI entry point") and checklist status-4, so this is a clarity gap rather than a coverage gap; naming those two assertions explicitly in the fixture step would remove any implementer discretion.

Measurement and data obligations are recorded as inapplicable by the accepted Implementation Plan (no quantitative target; no store, schema, retention, or migration change), so their absence as separate tasks is legitimate; the compatibility half is still owned by status-5 through the unchanged exit-code and byte-identical-record assertions.

status-8 (rollout and rollback) maps to cli-status-integration, which exercises the CLI status boundary but not the revert path itself. The proof is real-boundary for the displayed-status obligation; the rollback half rests on the accepted plan's statement that the mapper is a reversible local presentation change. Non-blocking, since the accepted Implementation Plan settles rollout as the existing CLI release and no separate rollback mechanism is in scope.

All eleven checklist obligations resolve to a single integration proof. That is defensible here because the accepted Implementation Plan states an isolated mapper test cannot prove the public wiring, and the slice enumerates discriminating assertions (other-job receipt, other-digest receipt, unauthenticated verdict, crash-before-binding, concurrent non-current job, failed read, exit-code baseline, byte-identical records, help text in the post-edit rerun) rather than one pass/fail signal.

Decision statuses account for every Recorded Decision in the accepted Implementation Plan, including atomic concurrent retry binding with crash behavior and the failed-read unavailability contract; none is reopened or restated with altered terms. Data and measurement categories are recorded as inapplicable by the accepted plan, so no placeholder owners are required.

Slice 1 completion signal is narrower than the accepted scope: "Pending and Approved pass through the CLI entry point and the status help text names those two states." The accepted ticket, Product Plan, and Implementation Plan contract require exactly three CLI statuses (Pending, Approved, Rejected) with actual blocking findings, and checklist status-1 and status-9 require all three states including help text. As written the slice can be declared complete while Rejected is never displayed and the help text omits it, so the accepted user-facing claim can be falsely reported as satisfied. Restate the completion signal to require every applicable proof to pass after the final edit and to cover all three statuses.

The single proof specification is non-discriminating for most accepted scenarios. Slice 1's steps say "The integration fixture covers Pending and Approved states," and the first RED only names "the missing Pending/Approved assertions," yet cli-status-integration is the Required proof for every checklist row, including status-4 ("Prove all six accepted scenarios through the CLI and coordinator") and status-7 (stale/missing receipts and preserved findings). Accepted scenarios 3 through 6 (Rejected with actual findings, stale receipt cannot approve, interrupted review Pending with actual error and retry, finished review without a valid receipt Pending with actual receipt error and no invented findings) can all be broken while the named command still passes. Name the fixture assertions for each of the six scenarios, including the stale-receipt and both failure-path retry assertions required by the accepted Implementation Plan contract.

Decision statuses are only partially mapped. The plan records a single entry ("the Implementation Plan's existing coordinator/receipt source of truth is unchanged") while the accepted Implementation Plan records additional load-bearing decisions: job-identifier plus plan-digest binding of the display, verbatim pass-through of recorded rejection findings with no synthesized reasons, retry creating a new review for repaired or unchanged bytes with history as non-authority, atomic retry binding with crash-before-binding leaving the prior terminal state visible and never falsely Approved, running review displays Pending, and interrupted or receipt-missing displays Pending with actual error and retry. Each applicable Recorded Decision needs an explicit status of unchanged.

The documentation obligation (status-9, CLI status help text for all three states) maps to cli-status-integration, but no step names a help-text assertion or the accepted surface entrypoint `status --help`. Even with the scope corrections above, state the help-text assertion explicitly so the documentation obligation resolves to a real boundary rather than inference.

Slicing decision, rationale, slice prerequisites (explicitly none), and relies_on_unmerged_successor: false are all stated and defensible for this cohesive presentation change; no dependency-ordering or pull-request-decomposition problem was found. The failures above are execution mechanics only, so repair stays in plan-execution.

Slice 1 proof scope contradicts the accepted proof boundary: the slice states "The integration fixture covers Pending and Approved states" while the accepted Implementation Plan requires "Exercise all six accepted scenarios through the real CLI and coordinator boundary, including a stale receipt, actual rejection findings, interrupted retry, and finished receipt-missing retry." Checklist item status-4 ("Prove all six accepted scenarios") and status-7 ("Reject stale or missing approval receipts and preserve actual findings") both resolve to cli-status-integration, so the only named proof is non-discriminating for them: scenarios 3, 4, 5, and 6 can be entirely broken or absent while the named command exits 0. Specify the fixture assertions for each of the six accepted scenarios, including the actual rejection findings, the stale-receipt non-approval, and both Pending-with-actual-error retry paths that bind a new current job without changing plan bytes.

Slice 1 completion signal is weaker than the accepted behavior it must gate: "Pending and Approved pass through the CLI entry point and the status help text names those two states." The accepted spec defines exactly three statuses and checklist item status-9 obligates "Update CLI status help text for all three states" over the accepted surface entrypoint `status --help`. Two reasonable implementations satisfy this completion text — one shipping Rejected and one omitting it — and the omitting one would falsely report the accepted user-facing claim (a builder can distinguish all three current outcomes) as satisfied. Restate completion so every applicable proof passes after the final edit and the help text names Pending, Approved, and Rejected.

The first RED step is not startable for the uncovered scenarios: it instructs adding "the failing tests/integration/review-status.test.ts fixture with all integration assertions described below," but the only assertions described below are the Pending and Approved ones. The implementer must invent the fixture actors, receipt binding, and expected assertions for rejection findings, stale receipt, interruption, and receipt-missing retry. Name each fixture's real actor boundary (coordinator job identifier and plan digest, authenticated receipt), edit action, and expected exit or assertion before any production edit.

Decision status is recorded as a single prose sentence covering only the coordinator/receipt source of truth. The accepted Implementation Plan also records load-bearing decisions on atomic retry binding and crash-before-binding behavior ("A crash before that binding leaves the prior terminal state visible and retryable, never falsely Approved"). Record an explicit unchanged status entry for each Recorded Decision so no accepted decision is silently dropped.

Slicing decision is explicit (one pull request, one slice, prerequisites stated as none, no unmerged-successor reliance) and the rationale rests on conceptual cohesion rather than size. That part of the plan is sound; no slicing repair is requested.

Slice 1 proof scope is non-discriminating. The first-RED step states "The integration fixture covers Pending and Approved states" and the only proof (cli-status-integration) is defined by that fixture. Scenarios 3 (Rejected with those actual findings), 4 (stale approval cannot approve a repaired plan), 5 (interrupted review shows Pending with its actual error and retries without changing plan bytes), and 6 (finished nonblocking review without a valid receipt shows Pending with the actual receipt error, no invented rejection findings, retry without changing plan bytes) have no named assertion.
